title: The Moravians' hundred-year prayer
hookLine: at Herrnhut, a quarrelsome refugee village starts a prayer watch that tradition says ran for a century

lines: A REFUGE TURNS INTO AN ARGUMENT.
cards: On a nobleman's estate in Saxony, a village is going up fast. The newcomers are religious refugees, some from Moravia, joined by others with their own convictions and their own grudges.
The estate belongs to a young count named Zinzendorf, shaped by the Pietists we met yesterday, and he's let them settle. They call the place Herrnhut.
Almost at once, they're fighting: about doctrine, about leadership, about who's right. A refuge has turned into an argument. Zinzendorf goes house to house, talking, listening, pleading.
Then something changes, and out of the change comes a prayer that, tradition says, didn't stop for a century.

teach.h: MADE ONE AT THE LORD'S TABLE.
teach.b: The Moravian story remembers the turn this way. After months of quarrels, the community agrees on a shared way of living together, and then gathers for communion.
Those present later described a deep sense of being made one, forgiven and reconciled, at the Lord's table. Soon after, a small group of men and women decide to keep a watch of prayer.
Each person takes an hour, linked one into the next, so that at any time of day or night, someone in Herrnhut is praying.
Tradition says the chain kept going for about a hundred years, passed from one generation to the next.

teach.h: THE FIRE SHALL NEVER GO OUT.
teach.b: Later tellings link the idea to an old command about the altar in Leviticus, in the King James words: "The fire shall ever be burning upon the altar; it shall never go out."
In Hebrew, that's esh tamid, a fire that is always there. The Moravians weren't keeping a flame on stone. They were keeping prayer alive in people.
Isaiah has a picture for it too: "I have set watchmen upon thy walls, O Jerusalem, which shall never hold their peace day nor night."
No one person prayed for a hundred years, or through every night. Each took one hour, and trusted the others with the rest.
The watch worked only because it was shared, and a quarreling village became a community that took turns holding the world before God.
Out of that same community, missionaries soon went out across the seas, and some of them, as tomorrow's story shows, ended up on a ship in a storm.

how: Some Christian communities still keep a prayer watch the way Herrnhut did: people sign up for hours on a shared schedule so that someone is praying at every hour, day and night.

practice: Let these few minutes be one hour of the watch, in miniature.
Breathe in, and bring to mind someone who needs to be held; breathe out, and keep them there, praying for them if you pray, or holding them in your attention if you don't.
